section.title: Oracles against Babylon, Edom, and Arabia
section.sectionRationale: Three short, urgent oracles are gathered here within the wider collection against the nations, chapters 13 to 23: a dire vision of Babylon's fall witnessed by a posted watchman, a brief and haunting exchange with a watchman about Edom's uncertain night, and a warning of Arabia's caravans fleeing for their lives. Each shows the LORD's word breaking in on history with unbearable weight.
section.thesis: The LORD who shows His prophet Babylon's sudden fall, who answers Edom's watchman with an unresolved word about the coming night, and who scatters Arabia's caravans before the sword, proves that no power, however established, stands outside His announced and certain judgments.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: the dire vision against the Desert by the Sea and the prophet's anguish; the watchman's cry, Fallen, fallen is Babylon; the brief oracle against Dumah, what is left of the night; and the oracle against Arabia's fleeing caravans.

units.label: The burden against the Desert by the Sea
units.note: a dire vision, the prophet in anguish

verses.text: This is the burden against the Desert by the Sea: Like whirlwinds sweeping through the Negev, an invader comes from the desert, from a land of terror.
A dire vision is declared to me: “The traitor still betrays, and the destroyer still destroys. Go up, O Elam! Lay siege, O Media! I will put an end to all her groaning.”
Therefore my body is filled with anguish. Pain grips me, like the pains of a woman in labor. I am bewildered to hear, I am dismayed to see.
My heart falters; fear makes me tremble. The twilight of my desire has turned to horror.
They prepare a table, they lay out a carpet, they eat, they drink! Rise up, O princes, oil the shields!

units.label: The watchman's cry: Fallen, fallen is Babylon
units.note: the sudden report from the watchtower

verses.text: For this is what the Lord says to me: “Go, post a {{tsaphah|lookout}} and have him report what he sees.
When he sees chariots with teams of horsemen, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, he must be alert, fully alert.”
Then the lookout shouted: “Day after day, my lord, I stand on the watchtower; night after night I stay at my post.
Look, here come the riders, horsemen in pairs.” And one answered, saying: “{{naphal|Fallen}}, fallen is Babylon! All the images of her gods lie shattered on the ground!”
O my people, crushed on the threshing floor, I tell you what I have heard from the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel.

units.label: The burden against Dumah
units.note: what is left of the night

verses.text: This is the burden against Dumah: One calls to me from Seir, “Watchman, what is left of the night? Watchman, what is left of the night?”
The watchman replies, “Morning has come, but also the night. If you would inquire, then inquire. Come back yet again.”
This is the burden against Arabia: In the thickets of Arabia you must lodge, O caravans of Dedanites.
Bring water for the thirsty, O dwellers of Tema; meet the refugees with food.
For they flee from the sword, the sword that is drawn, from the bow that is bent, and from the stress of battle.
For this is what the Lord says to me: “Within one year, as a hired worker would count it, all the glory of Kedar will be gone.
The remaining archers, the warriors of Kedar, will be few.” For the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken.

tsaphah.gloss: To watch, to keep lookout. A tsaphah, watchman, stood on a city's walls or towers to give early warning of danger, a role Isaiah himself performs here for Judah, straining to see and report what the LORD reveals to him even when the vision brings him anguish.

naphal.gloss: To fall, to collapse. The doubled cry, fallen, fallen, is Babylon, uses this verb twice for emphasis, a shout of astonished finality that Scripture echoes centuries later over the fall of a still greater Babylon, the world's opposition to God, Revelation 14:8, 18:2.

basic.context: This chapter gathers three short, intense oracles: a dire vision of Babylon's fall so vivid it leaves Isaiah in physical anguish, a haunting two-line exchange about Edom's uncertain night, and a warning that Arabia's caravans must flee for their lives before an advancing sword. Each shows that the LORD's word about the nations is not academic; it costs the prophet who carries it real distress.
basic.hermeneutics: The Babylon oracle likely anticipates its fall to the Medes and Elamites (Persians), fulfilled when Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BC; the brief Dumah oracle addresses Edom with a deliberately unresolved answer, and Arabia's oracle predicts a specific, dateable defeat of Kedar within a year. These are concrete historical judgments, not merely symbolic; their unresolved and terse style, especially in the Dumah oracle, is itself part of the message; readers should not force more certainty onto it than the text offers.
basic.originalLanguages: Isaiah is told to set a tsaphah, a watchman, whose vigilant report climaxes in the doubled cry naphal, naphal, fallen, fallen is Babylon, an exclamation of shock later echoed word for word in Revelation over the fall of end-times Babylon. The repeated Hebrew verb underscores how total and sudden Babylon's collapse will be.
basic.typology: Isaiah as a watchman straining to see and faithfully report even a terrifying vision foreshadows the prophetic office fulfilled and surpassed in Christ, the faithful witness who sees and declares the Father's word perfectly. The cry Fallen, fallen is Babylon anticipates the final fall of every proud human system opposed to God, announced again in Revelation.
basic.christ: The watchman's cry, Fallen, fallen is Babylon, is quoted almost verbatim in Revelation 14:8 and 18:2 of the final judgment on the world's opposition to God, a judgment Christ Himself will execute at His return. Isaiah's anguished, faithful witness to what he saw, even when it cost him distress, foreshadows Christ, the faithful and true witness, Revelation 3:14, who declares the Father's word without flinching.
basic.god: God reveals the future to His prophet even when the vision is dreadful, and He does not spare Isaiah the emotional cost of carrying such a word. He is sovereign over empires as different as Babylon, Edom, and Arabia, and His announced judgments arrive on His timetable, not theirs.
basic.crossReferences: Daniel 5 records history's most vivid single fulfillment of Babylon's sudden fall, in one night to the Medes and Persians. Revelation 14:8 and 18:2 quote this chapter's watchman cry over the final Babylon. Ezekiel 3:17 and 33:7 develop the watchman image further as a picture of prophetic responsibility. Hebrews 4:13 affirms that nothing is hidden from the God who reveals such things to His prophets.
basic.oneStory: These three oracles show the LORD's word breaking into history with real weight, both for the nations judged and for the prophet who bears the burden of announcing it. The watchman's cry over Babylon's fall becomes, in Revelation, the church's own confident hope that every proud opposition to God will finally and totally collapse before Christ.

context.literary:
The three oracles of Isaiah 21 are built like riddles. Each opens with the same heading, burden, in verses 1, 11 and 13, yet the first is named only by a puzzle, 'the Desert by the Sea,' and Babylon does not appear by name until the climax in verse 9. The second is named by a pun. The third is named plainly, but its answer is delivered as a dated countdown. Isaiah is teaching his hearers to listen for what is said, not only for what is named.

The first oracle is a study in perception. Verse 2 speaks of a vision declared to the prophet, verse 3 says he is 'bewildered to hear' and 'dismayed to see,' verses 6 and 7 are about what the lookout will see, verse 9 begins 'Look,' and verse 10 closes with 'what I have heard from the LORD.' Seeing and hearing are woven together, and the movement is from dread to report. Verses 1 to 5 form a vision that ends in a sudden cut: a banquet is laid, and in the same breath someone shouts for the princes to get up and oil the shields. The vision refuses to explain how a feast became a battle, which is exactly the point, because that is how Babylon's night would go.

Verse 6 and verse 16 both begin 'For this is what the Lord says to me,' and they frame the chapter's second half. Night is the other thread: the lookout stays at his post 'night after night,' verse 8, the Edomite voice asks what is left of the night, verse 11, and the answer is that morning comes and so does night, verse 12. The chapter closes on a formula of certainty, 'the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken,' verse 17, which answers the same title in verse 10.

The chapter also follows directly on Isaiah 20, where the prophet's body was itself the message, three years walking naked and barefoot as a sign against Egypt and Cush, Isaiah 20:2-3. In chapter 21 the body speaks again, in the labor pains and trembling of verses 3 and 4.
context.historical:
In Isaiah's own day Babylon was not yet the master of the east. She was a restless city that sometimes bowed to Assyria and sometimes rebelled, and her king Merodach-baladan sent envoys to Hezekiah, Isaiah 39:1. The vision therefore reaches ahead, and the best known fulfilment is the night of October 539 BC when Babylon fell to the forces of Cyrus. Elam lay east of Babylon, and Media beyond it, so the call 'Go up, O Elam! Lay siege, O Media!' names the two powers that stand behind the Persian conquest. Isaiah 13:17 says the same, 'I will stir up against them the Medes,' and Jeremiah 51:11 agrees. The Greek historian Herodotus tells of Persians entering by the bed of the river that ran through the city while Babylon kept a festival, which fits the table and the carpet of verse 5. Scripture's own account is in Daniel 5, a feast for a thousand nobles with wine drunk from the temple vessels, ending 'that very night,' Daniel 5:30.

Dumah is one of the sons of Ishmael, Genesis 25:14, and the footnote of the BSB explains that the name is also a play on Edom and carries the sense of silence. Seir is another name for Edom, and Esau settled at Mount Seir, Genesis 36:8. Edom was a small mountain kingdom that lived under the shadow of the great powers for centuries, and the cry from Seir sounds like a people asking whether their long subjection will end.

The third oracle moves into the desert trade routes. Dedan appears among the descendants of Abraham, Genesis 25:3, Tema and Kedar among the sons of Ishmael, Genesis 25:13 and 25:15. Kedar's tents became a byword for desert life, Psalm 120:5 and Song of Songs 1:5, and Kedar's flocks were sold to Tyre, Ezekiel 27:21. These tribes ran caravans through country that Assyria and then Babylon pressed hard, and Jeremiah 49:28 names Kedar as a target of Nebuchadnezzar. The phrase 'as a hired worker would count it,' verse 16, appears again in Isaiah 16:14, where Moab is given three years: a worker watches the calendar closely, and so does the LORD.
context.canonical:
Isaiah 21 sits inside the long gallery of oracles against the nations, and it looks back to the opening of that gallery. Isaiah 13:1 begins with a burden against Babylon, and verse 19 calls her 'the jewel of the kingdoms' to be overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah. Chapter 21 compresses that same fall into a single night. The theme returns later in the book when Bel and Nebo crouch under the weight of their own idols, Isaiah 46:1, and when the virgin daughter of Babylon is told to sit in the dust, Isaiah 47:1. Jeremiah then carries the story forward, 'Suddenly Babylon has fallen and been shattered,' Jeremiah 51:8.

The watchman is a figure the prophets keep returning to. Habakkuk takes his post on the ramparts to see what the LORD will say, Habakkuk 2:1-3. Ezekiel is made a watchman and warned that he is accountable for the blood of those he fails to warn, Ezekiel 33:6-7. Isaiah himself will later condemn Israel's watchmen as blind and mute, Isaiah 56:10, and promise watchmen who never fall silent over Jerusalem, Isaiah 62:6. The writer of Psalm 130:6 uses the lookout waiting for dawn as a picture of the soul waiting on the Lord.

In the New Testament the doubled cry is taken up by an angel. Revelation 14:8 gives it as 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great,' and Revelation 18:2 adds the ruin that follows. Babylon has become the name of every proud, seductive world order. Jesus' own repeated command to keep watch, Matthew 24:42 and Mark 13:35-37, carries the lookout's duty to the church.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wanted his hearers to learn three things from a chapter that is mostly fear. First, that the empires which seem to decide history are on a schedule that is not their own. Judah in the late eighth century, tempted to look to Babylon as a possible ally against Assyria, Isaiah 39:1-2, needed to hear that Babylon's glory was borrowed and brief. Second, that what he reports is not his own forecast but something he has been given: 'I tell you what I have heard from the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel,' verse 10. His fear is the evidence that he does not enjoy the message. Third, that the small nations on Judah's borders are not forgotten. Edom's anxious question and Arabia's refugees are taken seriously by God, who sends an answer to the one and an instruction of mercy for the other, 'Bring water for the thirsty,' verse 14.

The chapter also trains its hearers in patience with partial answers. The watchman's reply in verse 12 is not a failure of the oracle. It is the oracle, and it asks the questioner to come back and keep asking.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The chapter reports what a watchman saw and what he was told to say. It does not instruct modern readers to look for the same nations in today's headlines, and it does not hand out a formula for dating the future. What it does model can be carried over: God's people are to stand at their post, report faithfully what they have heard, and refuse to look away from a hard word. The one direct command in the chapter is not about politics at all. The dwellers of Tema are told to bring water to the thirsty and to meet refugees with food, verse 14, and that care for people fleeing violence is a direct instruction that stands even while the oracle announces judgment on the wider region. The riddle of verse 12 describes the situation of someone who asks God about the future and receives a partial answer; it does not tell believers to expect riddles as the normal way God speaks.

debates.question: What is Edom being told when the watchman says, 'Morning has come, but also the night'?

views.label: Respite followed by renewed oppression
views.case: The Hebrew verb for 'has come' is a perfect form of 'to come,' and it can be read either way, as 'is coming' or 'has come.' On this reading the watchman gives real news, a morning, and a warning that night follows. Edom's history under Assyria, Babylon and later powers swung between relief and fresh subjection, and the answer fits that unsettled pattern.

views.label: A deliberate refusal to give a full forecast
views.case: The reply ends with an invitation, 'If you would inquire, then inquire. Come back yet again,' and says nothing about dates or powers. On this reading the vagueness is intended. Edom is not given the comfort of a timetable, and the open door is the only real answer.

views.label: Judgment and deliverance together for the nations
views.case: Some read 'morning' as the dawn of the LORD's rule and 'night' as the judgment that must come first. Isaiah often speaks of a day that is darkness for the proud and light for the humble, and the riddle may hold both in one breath.

debates.bearing: All three readings agree that the oracle gives less certainty than the questioner wanted and that it still counts as the word of the LORD. The safest posture is to read it as an honest invitation to keep seeking, not as a coded prediction.

debates.question: Which fall of Babylon does the watchman announce, and when?

views.label: The Persian conquest of 539 BC
views.case: Elam and Media are named as the attackers, Isaiah 13:17 and Jeremiah 51:11 name the Medes, and the feast in verse 5 matches Daniel 5. Verse 9 adds that the images of Babylon's gods lie shattered, which suits a city captured while its gods were being praised, Daniel 5:4. Most readers who treat the chapter as prophecy of a future event take this view.

views.label: An earlier Assyrian blow
views.case: Babylon was besieged and later sacked by Sennacherib in the decades after Isaiah's ministry began. Some scholars link the vision to Assyrian pressure on Babylon in Isaiah's own lifetime, noting that Elam was often a partner of Babylon, which complicates the picture.

views.label: A pattern, fulfilled in stages
views.case: The doubled 'fallen' is picked up in Revelation 14:8 and 18:2 for a final Babylon, so the oracle has a shape that reaches past any one event. Babylon's falls, ancient and still to come, are one pattern of pride answered by the LORD.

debates.bearing: The text's own pointers, Elam, Media and the feast, favour the Persian conquest as the first fulfilment, while Revelation shows the pattern continuing. Readers should hold the identification of the event with some humility and the message of the oracle with firm confidence.

study.originalLanguages:
The heading in verses 1, 11 and 13 is massa, usually translated burden, from a verb meaning to lift or carry. It can mean a load carried by a beast, Isaiah 46:1 uses the related idea of idols weighing down animals, and it also names a prophetic message that weighs on the one who must deliver it. In this chapter both senses meet. Isaiah carries a message that presses on his body, verses 3 and 4, and the oracle presses on the nations it addresses.

Verse 2 uses two participles from the same sound family, boged, the traitor, and shoded, the destroyer. The verbs are bagad, to act treacherously, and shadad, to devastate. The pair is not a pointless doubling. Isaiah 33:1 uses the same two roots with the sentence reversed: 'When you have finished destroying, you will be destroyed. When you have finished betraying, you will be betrayed.' The empire that betrays and destroys in verse 2 is being told, in advance, that the roles will be exchanged. The same root of treachery, bagad, drives the grim refrain of Isaiah 24:16.

The name Dumah in verse 11 has a second meaning, which the BSB footnote notes: silence. The noun duma is the word of the grave in Psalm 94:17, 'the abode of silence,' and Psalm 115:17, 'nor any who descend into silence.' Dumah is also the name of a son of Ishmael, Genesis 25:14. Isaiah uses a real name with a heavy overtone, so that a land of silence asks a question into the dark and gets only a watchman's riddle.

In verse 12 the watchman says 'Morning has come, but also the night.' The verb is the perfect of 'to come,' and Hebrew perfects often describe something so certain that it is spoken of as already done. That is why translators divide between 'has come' and 'is coming.' The answer is both present and future at once.

In verse 16 the phrase 'as a hired worker would count it' uses the word for a hired hand, sakir. Job 7:1-2 pictures such a worker longing for his wages, and Isaiah 16:14 uses the very same phrase of Moab. A hired worker does not round his days. The exactness is the point: the LORD's year will be a calendar year, not a figure of speech.

Finally, the BSB footnote on verse 8 records a textual difficulty. The Dead Sea Scrolls and the Syriac read 'lookout' where the Masoretic Text has 'lion.' The older English reading, 'he cried, A lion,' follows the Masoretic Text, as though the watchman roared his report. Either way the watchman speaks with force.

typology.type: The watchman who does not sleep, Isaiah 21:8
typology.fulfillment: The lookout stays at his post night after night, and his duty is to see the danger and cry out. Ezekiel is told the same, Ezekiel 33:7, and he is held accountable if he stays silent. The pattern is fulfilled and sharpened in Jesus. In Gethsemane His soul is consumed with sorrow and He asks the disciples to keep watch, Mark 14:34, but they sleep, Matthew 26:40. He spent whole nights awake in prayer, Luke 6:12, and He commands the church to keep watch for His return, Mark 13:35-37. The type falls short in one place: the watchman only warns of the danger, while Christ stands in the way of it.

typology.type: The prophet's body in anguish, Isaiah 21:3-4
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah describes pain like a woman in labor, a falling heart and a trembling frame. He feels in his body what the word will do to others. The pattern is far larger in Christ, who is 'a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief,' Isaiah 53:3, and who wept over Jerusalem as the city refused Him, Luke 19:41-44. Paul has the same pattern in a lesser measure, 'deep sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart,' for his own people, Romans 9:2. The type escalates because the prophet shares a burden of sorrow, while Christ takes the burden of the judgment itself, Isaiah 53:11.

typology.type: Morning and night, the dawn that comes before the day, Isaiah 21:12
typology.fulfillment: The watchman's riddle is picked up in the New Testament as a description of the age believers live in. Zechariah sings that 'the Dawn will visit us from on high' to shine on those in darkness, Luke 1:78-79. Paul says 'The night is nearly over; the day has drawn near,' Romans 13:12, and Peter speaks of the prophetic word as a lamp in a dark place 'until the day dawns and the morning star rises,' 2 Peter 1:19. Jesus calls Himself 'the bright Morning Star,' Revelation 22:16. The morning has come with His first coming and the night is not yet over, which is exactly the double answer of verse 12. This is a pattern in the language, not a claim that Isaiah's riddle was about Christ.

typology.type: Refugees fed and given water, Isaiah 21:14
typology.fulfillment: The dwellers of Tema are told to meet fleeing people with water and food. Jesus makes the same act a measure of loyalty to Himself: 'I was thirsty and you gave Me drink,' Matthew 25:35, and 'a cup of cold water' given to a disciple will not lose its reward, Matthew 10:42. He knew the other side of it as well, for the child Jesus was taken by night into Egypt to escape a sword that was searching for Him, Matthew 2:13-14. The echo is real but loose. It points to the heart of the command, not to a fulfilled prediction.

study.christ:
The chapter reaches Christ most clearly by way of its two great images, the night and the watchman. The riddle of verse 12, morning and night together, is the shape of the age that opened when Jesus came. The Dawn from on high has visited, Luke 1:78-79, and Jesus is the bright Morning Star, Revelation 22:16, and yet Paul still tells believers that the night is nearly over, not that it is gone, Romans 13:12. Edom's question, how much of the night remains, is the question of the whole church between the cross and the return, and the answer is still 'keep watching.'

The second link is the pattern of the one who carries a burden in his own body. Isaiah is shaken to the point of trembling by what he sees. Jesus does the same in Gethsemane, 'My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death,' Mark 14:34, and asks for watchers who fall asleep. The watchman who stays awake is the Lord Himself. His sorrow over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41-44, is the sorrow of a prophet who knows a city is about to fall, and yet it goes further than any prophet's. Isaiah's later portrait of the Servant, 'a man of sorrows,' Isaiah 53:3, shows that the One who sees the judgment is the One who will carry it, Isaiah 53:11.

A third link runs through the desert peoples of the third oracle. Kedar and Nebaioth are Ishmael's sons, Genesis 25:13, and Isaiah 60:7 promises that 'all the flocks of Kedar will be gathered to you' and 'go up on My altar with acceptance.' The wise men who came from the east with gold and frankincense, Matthew 2:11, and the Arabs present at Pentecost, Acts 2:11, are early signs of that gathering. The sword that sends the caravans fleeing in verse 15 is answered by a Savior who is, in His own childhood, a refugee, Matthew 2:13-14.

A word of care. The chapter never names the Messiah, and the links above rest on what the New Testament itself says about night, watching and the nations. The fall of Babylon is carried into Revelation, where the Lamb triumphs over the beast and its allies, Revelation 17:14, and that victory is the true meaning of the shattered images in verse 9.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows about God is that He speaks to particular people about particular nights. The word comes 'to me,' verses 2, 6 and 16, and the prophet is placed in the story as a human being with a body that trembles. God does not use Isaiah as a loudspeaker. The message is carried by a man who is allowed to be afraid, and the fear is part of the evidence that the word is not his invention.

He is Lord of timetables. A hired worker counts days with care, and the LORD announces the end of Kedar's glory on a countdown of exactly that kind, verse 16. Elsewhere the book says that He declares the end from the beginning, Isaiah 46:10, and here it is shown in small and large events alike: a night that will end Babylon, a year that will empty Kedar. Yet He is not a distant clockmaker. He fills the vision with rushing detail, a table and a carpet and a call to oil the shields, and He lets a lookout name the exact thing he sees.

He is judge of idols. The announcement 'All the images of her gods lie shattered on the ground,' verse 9, treats Babylon's gods as nothing, and the book later mocks Bel and Nebo as burdens that animals must carry, Isaiah 46:1. The God of Israel does not compete with them as an equal. He simply speaks and they lie broken.

He is patient with the one who asks. To the voice from Seir He gives neither a refusal nor a forecast, but an open door, 'If you would inquire, then inquire. Come back yet again,' verse 12. The same God who announces judgment on Edom's neighbors is willing to be asked by Edom. He is also merciful in the middle of judgment. In the very oracle that scatters Arabia's caravans He commands the people of Tema to bring water for the thirsty and to meet the refugees with food, verse 14.

For worship the chapter teaches watching as a posture. Psalm 130:6 gives the same picture from the other side, a soul that waits for the Lord 'more than watchmen wait for the morning,' and it ends in confidence about redemption. The God who names night and morning in one sentence is the God to wait for.

crossReferences.note: The opening oracle of the whole collection names the Medes as the army the LORD will stir up against Babylon and calls her 'the jewel of the kingdoms.' Isaiah 21 returns to the same event with the view from a watchtower, so the two chapters read as a wide shot and a close-up of the same night.

A direct reversal of the pair in Isaiah 21:2: the destroyer who has not been destroyed and the traitor who has not been betrayed will, when they finish, receive the same treatment. It shows that the empire's own methods become its sentence.

Bel and Nebo, the chief gods of Babylon, crouch and cower while their images are loaded onto animals. It fills in the picture behind 'the images of her gods lie shattered' in Isaiah 21:9 and shows idols as burdens that must be carried, not gods that carry.

Jeremiah takes up the sudden fall, 'Babylon has fallen and been shattered,' and adds a call to flee from her, because 'we tried to heal Babylon, but she could not be healed.' It extends Isaiah's watchman cry into an urgent summons for God's people to leave.

A feast for a thousand nobles, with wine drunk from the temple vessels and praise of gods of gold and silver. The details line up with the table and carpet of Isaiah 21:5, where eating and drinking is interrupted by a call to arms, and they are followed by the night of Daniel 5:30.

Habakkuk takes his stand on the ramparts to see what the LORD will say. The answer tells him to write the vision, because it 'awaits an appointed time' and 'will surely come.' It gives the watchman's patience a theology that Isaiah 21:8 acts out.

The watchman who sees the sword and does not blow the horn is held accountable for the blood of those who die. It explains why Isaiah is told to post a lookout and to report everything he sees, and why an honest report is a matter of life and death.

The psalmist's soul waits for the Lord 'more than watchmen wait for the morning.' Where Isaiah 21:12 gives the night's riddle, this psalm gives the heart of the person who is waiting through it, and it ends on a note of plentiful redemption.

The same phrase, 'as a hired worker counts the years,' is used for Moab. Set beside Isaiah 21:16, it shows a repeated way in which the LORD fixes the end of a nation's pride on a specific schedule, whether three years for Moab or one for Kedar.

Kedar, Dumah and Tema stand in the same list as sons of Ishmael. Isaiah 21's second and third oracles are therefore addressed to Abraham's own extended family, and the later promise of Isaiah 60:7 that Kedar's flocks will come to the altar fits the same family.

The angel cries 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!' and then describes her as a lair for demons. It shows that the watchman's cry in Isaiah 21:9 became the church's language for the end of every arrogant and seductive world system.

Jesus tells His disciples to keep watch because they do not know the day their Lord will come. It turns Isaiah's watchman, standing night after night at his post, into the pattern for every believer who waits for the return of the Lord.

study.oneStory:
Babylon begins in Genesis. Babel is the city built by people who wanted a name for themselves, and the LORD scattered them, Genesis 11:9. Everything after that is a long argument between two cities, the one that exalts itself and the one that waits on the LORD. Isaiah 21 sits at a hinge in that argument. The proud city is announced as fallen, long before it has become the empire that will carry Judah away, and the lookout who sees it is a reminder that God tells His people the end before they live through the middle.

The chapter also reaches back to a family. Dumah, Kedar and Tema are sons of Ishmael, Genesis 25:13-15, and Edom is Esau, Jacob's brother, Genesis 36:8. These are not strangers to the story of Abraham. They are relatives who went elsewhere, and the oracles show God still reading their names aloud. The hurts of those relationships continue through the prophets. Obadiah accuses Edom of violence against his brother Jacob, Obadiah 1:10. Yet the book of Isaiah ends up promising that the flocks of Kedar and Nebaioth will go up on God's altar with acceptance, Isaiah 60:7.

The story's turning point is the faithful watchman who also carries the burden. Jesus keeps vigil where His friends cannot, Mark 14:34, bears the sorrow that Isaiah only tasted, Isaiah 53:3, and rises as the Dawn from on high, Luke 1:78-79. The church lives in the strange period of the riddle, when morning has come and night is still around, and its calling is to keep watch, Mark 13:35-37.

The story ends with the cry becoming a reality. Revelation 18:2 announces the fall of the last Babylon, and the Lamb triumphs, Revelation 17:14. In the new creation the gates of the city stand open and 'the glory and honor of the nations' is brought in, Revelation 21:26, so that the families once on the wrong side of the walls come home. Night is gone, because the city has no need of lamps, for the glory of God lights it, Revelation 21:23. The question put to the watchman, what is left of the night, is finally answered by an unending day.

quiz.q: What effect does the dire vision of Babylon's fall have on Isaiah himself?

options.text: It fills him with physical anguish, like the pains of a woman in labor.
options.note: Verses 3 to 4 describe exactly this bodily, emotional cost of receiving the vision.

options.text: It leaves him completely unaffected and calm.
options.note: The opposite; the text describes real, visceral distress.

options.text: It makes him celebrate immediately with joy.
options.note: His response is anguish and dismay, not celebration, at this point in the text.

options.text: It causes him to doubt the vision's truth.
options.note: He does not doubt the vision; he is distressed by its content, not skeptical of its reality.

quiz.q: What does the watchman finally report in verse 9?

options.text: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and her idols lie shattered on the ground.
options.note: This is the watchman's climactic report, word for word.

options.text: Babylon has successfully repelled all invaders.
options.note: The opposite; Babylon has fallen, not triumphed.

options.text: The riders have turned back without engaging Babylon.
options.note: Not what is reported; the riders' arrival signals Babylon's fall.

options.text: Babylon has surrendered peacefully with no violence.
options.note: The fall is described starkly, with shattered idols, suggesting real violence, not a peaceful surrender.

quiz.q: How does the watchman answer Dumah's repeated question, what is left of the night?

options.text: Morning has come, but also the night, and he invites further inquiry.
options.note: Verse 12 gives exactly this brief, deliberately unresolved answer.

options.text: He gives a full, detailed timeline of coming events.
options.note: The opposite; his answer is notably terse and incomplete.

options.text: He refuses to answer at all.
options.note: He does answer, briefly, rather than remaining silent.

options.text: He promises the night will never end.
options.note: His answer includes morning as well as night, not unending darkness alone.

quiz.q: What warning is given concerning Arabia and Kedar?

options.text: Within one year, Kedar's glory and warriors will be greatly diminished.
options.note: Verses 16 to 17 give this specific, dated warning.

options.text: Kedar will conquer all its neighboring nations within the year.
options.note: The opposite; Kedar's own glory is said to fade, not expand.

options.text: Arabia will be spared from any conflict indefinitely.
options.note: The passage instead describes caravans fleeing the sword, not peace.

options.text: The Dedanites will conquer Tema within the year.
options.note: The text describes refugees fleeing and being aided, not one Arabian people conquering another.

quiz.q: How does the watchman's cry over Babylon connect to the New Testament?

options.text: Revelation quotes it almost word for word over the final fall of the world's opposition to God.
options.note: Revelation 14:8 and 18:2 both echo Fallen, fallen is Babylon directly.

options.text: The New Testament never mentions Babylon again.
options.note: The opposite; Babylon becomes a major symbol in Revelation.

options.text: It is only referenced once, in a minor footnote in Acts.
options.note: It is a major, repeated theme in Revelation, not a minor footnote elsewhere.

options.text: It refers exclusively to the literal ancient city with no further significance.
options.note: The ancient city's fall is real, but Revelation gives the phrase a further, symbolic significance for the end of all opposition to God.

questions: Isaiah's true vision from God brought him real anguish, not comfort. Has faithfully facing a hard truth ever cost you more than you expected?
The watchman stood at his post day after day, night after night, before finally seeing what he was watching for. Where do you need patient, faithful watchfulness rather than a quick answer right now?
Edom's watchman gave a brief, unresolved answer: morning has come, but also the night. How do you handle situations in life where God does not give you the full, clear answer you want?
Babylon's idols lay shattered when she fell. What false securities or idols in your own life might God be exposing as unable to stand?

The cry Fallen, fallen is Babylon becomes, in Revelation, a shout of hope for God's people. How does knowing that every power opposed to God will finally fall change how you face discouragement today?

translationNotes.note: Desert by the Sea is a poetic name for Babylon, likely referring to the marshy plain around the Tigris and Euphrates, or symbolically evoking chaos and vastness.

Dumah may be both a place name, an Arabian oasis, and a wordplay on the Hebrew word for silence, and on Edom, since it is spelled almost identically; the terse oracle suits either or both associations.
